extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity professionals, and science journalists
extracted.subtask_description: An archive/category page collecting news stories about retractions from Springer Nature journals and books, summarizing causes, investigative triggers, and publisher responses. Useful for understanding what practices and problems prompt retraction or integrity investigations at a major publisher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions about the data / data integrity concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions prompted after a reader raised questions about the data (e.g., 'a reader raised questions about the data' led to retraction of a paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a 2023 BMC Psychology paper was retracted after readers queried the data underpinning reported findings; data concerns are a common trigger for publisher investigation and retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated or fake references
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that contain references to works that do not exist (e.g., 'the book had multiple references to works that do not exist').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Springer Nature book on machine learning was retracted after Retraction Watch reported fake references. Fabricated citations undermine the scholarly record and can prompt removal of a title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship irregularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems related to authorship such as disputed authorship, inappropriate attribution, or other authorship-related issues (noted as 'authorship... issues').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a journal retracted 16 papers after a whistleblower flagged 'irregularities' including authorship concerns; authorship problems are cited as a standalone reason for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromised peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review processes that were compromised or irregular, cited as a cause for retraction (phrasing: 'compromised peer review').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: publisher notices attributing retractions to compromised peer review. Such failures can lead to mass retractions across issues when peer-review integrity is in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulation or rotation of images indicating possible data fabrication or falsification (e.g., 'manipulation and rotation of images').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Oncogene retracted multiple articles after a 2014 investigation that found manipulated and rotated images; image manipulation is treated as evidence of intentional or reckless misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial overlap / duplicate publication / plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial overlap between works (quoted as 'substantial overlap') leading to retraction for redundancy or self-plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Two flood-prediction papers were retracted for 'substantial overlap' between the works; overlap can prompt contested retractions when content is not sufficiently original or unique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate or irrelevant references
rubrics_metrics.description: References that are inappropriate or irrelevant to the work (stated as 'inappropriate or irrelevant references').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Publisher notices cite inappropriate/irrelevant references as one of the problems prompting investigation and retraction, often alongside other quality failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsensical phrases suggesting blind use of AI or poor machine translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of nonsensical phrases in manuscripts that suggest blind use of AI or machine-translation software (quoted: 'nonsensical phrases, suggesting blind use of AI or machine-translation software').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Notices pointing to nonsensical wording have been used as evidence manuscripts were produced without adequate human oversight; this can trigger retractions or suspensions of submission types (e.g., letters/commentaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-generated manuscripts / LLM-produced content
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts that appear to be generated using large language models (LLMs) or other AI tools (phrasing: 'appeared to be generated using large language models (LLMs)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Neurosurgical Review retracted many commentaries/letters and paused accepting such submissions after an influx of content that appeared AI-generated; publishers may implement policies or pause submission types when AI-generated content is widespread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest editor misconduct or guest-editor-related failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems arising from guest editors that lead to mass retractions (noted as 'many from issues with guest editors').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Soft Computing retracted hundreds of papers, with retractions attributed in part to issues involving guest editors; journal editorial oversight and guest-editor practices are considered when evaluating integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive self-citation / citation manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns of aggressive self-citation or citation manipulation associated with certain institutions or authors (noted as 'engages in aggressive self-citation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Saveetha University was identified among affiliations with high retraction counts linked to aggressive self-citation practices; citation gaming can be part of broader integrity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistleblower / reader-flagged concerns as triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations and retractions initiated based on whistleblower or reader reports (phrasing: 'a whistleblower flagged it' and 'a concerned researcher... emailed each journal about problems').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Multiple retractions described here began after external parties alerted journals or Retraction Watch; journals often rely on external flags to begin integrity inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial note / pending investigation before retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may publish an editorial note informing readers they are looking into concerns prior to issuing a retraction (phrasing: 'editor's note informing readers the journal was looking into concerns about the data and conclusions').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Scientific Reports published an editor's note two years before retracting a controversial paper; editorial notes can signal an ongoing investigation and are part of the retraction process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher quality-control tools and confidential investigative processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers use tools for quality control and describe what prompts a research integrity investigation and what happens during such investigations (stated: 'the page outlines the tools the publisher uses for quality control, what prompts a research integrity investigation, and what happens during such investigations').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Springer Nature published data and a research-integrity page describing retraction counts and investigative triggers; publishers may keep investigation specifics confidential to avoid alerting those under inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass retractions with standardized notice language
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass retractions characterized by retraction notices that contain identical or similar wording across many papers (noted as 'the retraction notes contain identical language to notices in...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Several journals issued retractions with similar phrasing after identifying systemic issues (e.g., compromised peer review, irrelevant references); recurring notice language can indicate coordinated, publisher-level investigation outcomes.
